statement: In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.
heath_proof: Let there be equal cones and cylinders of which the circles ABCD, EFGH are the bases; let AC, EG be the diameters of the bases, and KL, MN the axes, which are also the heights of the cones or cylinders; let the cylinders AO, EP be completed. I say that in the cylinders AO, EP the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights, that is, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL. For the height LK is either equal to the height MN or not equal. First, let it be equal. Now the cylinder AO is also equal to the cylinder EP. But cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases; [XII. 11] therefore the base ABCD is also equal to the base EFGH. Hence also, reciprocally, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL. Next, let the height LK not be equal to MN, but let MN be greater; from the height MN let QN be cut off equal to KL, through the point Q let the cylinder EP be cut by the plane TUS parallel to the planes of the circles EFGH, RP, and let the cylinder ES be conceived erected from the circle EFGH as base and with height NQ. Now, since the cylinder AO is equal to the cylinder EP, therefore, as the cylinder AO is to the cylinder ES, so is the cylinder EP to the cylinder ES. [V. 7] But, as the cylinder AO is to the cylinder ES, so is the base ABCD to the base EFGH, for the cylinders AO, ES are of the same height; [XII. 11] and, as the cylinder EP is to the cylinder ES, so is the height MN to the height QN, for the cylinder EP has been cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes. [XII. 13] Therefore also, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height QN. [V. 11] But the height QN is equal to the height KL; therefore, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL. Therefore in the cylinders AO, EP the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights. Next, in the cylinders AO, EP let the bases be reciprocally proportional to the heights, that is, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so let the height MN be to the height KL; I say that the cylinder AO is equal to the cylinder EP. For, with the same construction, since, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL, while the height KL is equal to the height QN, therefore, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height QN   But, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the cylinder AO to the cylinder ES, for they are of the same height; [XII. 11] and, as the height MN is to QN, so is the cylinder EP to the cylinder ES; [XII. 13] therefore, as the cylinder AO is to the cylinder ES, so is the cylinder EP to the cylinder ES. [V. 11] Therefore the cylinder AO is equal to the cylinder EP. [V. 9] And the same is true for the cones also.
ai_proof_text:
12.15
**Statement:** In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let AX and EO be two cones, or two cylinders. Let the circle ABCD with centre K be the base of AX and KL its axis, and let the circle EFGH with centre M be the base of EO and MN its axis. Each of the solids is comprehended by a right-angled triangle (for a cone) or a rectangle (for a cylinder) carried round one of the sides about the right angle, which remains fixed and is the axis, while the other side about the right angle describes the base [D11.18, D11.19, D11.20, D11.21, D11.22, D11.23]. Hence the angle AKL at K and the angle EMN at M are right angles, and the axes KL, MN are the heights of the solids. The bases are said to be reciprocally proportional to the heights when, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL [D6.2].

**Step 2.** Let the solids be so named that KL is not greater than MN. If KL is equal to MN, let P be the point N; if KL is less than MN, cut off from MN the straight line MP equal to KL [1.3]. In either case P lies on MN, MP is equal to KL, and the angle EMP, being the angle EMN, is right.

**Step 3.** Let ES be the cone, or the cylinder, of the same kind as AX and EO, comprehended by carrying round MP the right-angled triangle EMP, or the rectangle whose sides about the right angle at M are ME and MP [D11.18, D11.21]. Its axis is MP [D11.19, D11.22], and its base is the circle described by ME as it is carried round M in the plane at right angles to MP [D11.20, D11.23]; since MP lies along MN, this is the very circle EFGH described by ME carried round MN. Thus ES has the base EFGH and the height MP, which is equal to KL. When P is the point N, ES is the solid EO itself.

**Step 4.** The solids AX and ES are of the same height, since KL is equal to MP; therefore, as the solid AX is to the solid ES, so is the base ABCD to the base EFGH [12.11].

**Step 5.** The solids EO and ES stand on the same base EFGH; therefore, as the solid EO is to the solid ES, so is the height MN to the height MP [12.14]. (If P is the point N, ES is EO itself, and EO : ES and MN : MP are each the ratio of a magnitude to itself; any equimultiples of EO and MN then alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of any equimultiples of EO and MN respectively, so that these are the same ratio [D5.5].)

**Step 6.** Since MP is equal to KL, the same magnitude MN has to MP and to KL the same ratio [5.7]; therefore, as EO is to ES, so is MN to KL [5.11].

**Step 7.** First, let the solids AX and EO be equal. Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio; therefore, as AX is to ES, so is EO to ES [5.7]. But as AX is to ES, so is the base ABCD to the base EFGH (Step 4), and as EO is to ES, so is the height MN to the height KL (Step 6); therefore, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL [5.11]. Thus in the equal cones or cylinders AX, EO the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights.

**Step 8.** Conversely, let the bases be reciprocally proportional to the heights, that is, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so let the height MN be to the height KL. As ABCD is to EFGH, so is AX to ES (Step 4), and as MN is to KL, so is EO to ES (Step 6); therefore, as AX is to ES, so is EO to ES [5.11]. Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal to one another; therefore the solid AX is equal to the solid EO [5.9].

**Step 9.** Therefore, in equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal. Q.E.D.

Path note: for cylinders the auxiliary solid ES could instead be obtained by cutting EO with a plane through P parallel to its bases, cones then being handled separately through their ratio to the cylinders on the same bases; constructing ES directly on the base EFGH lets a single argument with 12.11 and 12.14 cover cones and cylinders together, and is the more direct route taken here.
